A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same modular SKB question-answering framework, renamed from FocusedRetriever to AF-Retriever. All 9 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including figures, tables, algorithms, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Tables 4–8 report original STaRK retrieval results, component experiments, and human-generated test-set results for FocusedRetriever.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A.5–A.6 report original AF-Retriever benchmark results, ablations, prediction-error analyses, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The hybrid retrieval, incremental candidate expansion, and three reranking strategies remain. V2 Algorithm 1 feeds predicted target type into Cypher generation, whereas v1 predicts it separately for the vector-retrieval branch. V2 also introduces progressive removal of relational context when reranking prompts overflow, addressing cases left unevaluated for relation-inclusive listwise reranking in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate multi-hop retrieval on the same PRIME, MAG, and AMAZON SKBs, using synthetic and human-generated questions. Larger test samples and experiments that modify prompts or model configurations remain within this dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds GraphRAFT comparisons on PRIME and MAG. It also retains only one of the two VSS+Reranker configurations reported in v1 Table 4. The remaining comparator membership, including the human-generated test comparisons, is substantially unchanged.

E3.justification: V1 explicitly restricts synthetic evaluation to 10%; v2 reports full-test evaluation and marks comparators available only on the 10% subset. The main backbone changes from LLaMA 3.3 70B to GPT OSS 120B, embeddings from ada-002 to text-embedding-3-small, and the candidate cap from 1,500,000 to 100. The retrieval mixture changes from 12 of 20 candidates to approximately two-thirds; new analyses introduce additional model, reasoning-effort, and candidate-cap configurations.

E4.justification: V2 adds a sequential pipeline ablation, multi-LLM prediction-error and reasoning-effort studies, candidate-cap sensitivity, relational-embedding ablations, node-type concealment experiments, and measured context-window and runtime analyses (Table 4 and Appendix A.6). The existing parsing, mixture-weight, and reranking studies are also expanded or revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's new runtime averages, medians, and maxima describe timing variation rather than uncertainty in experimental performance.

E6.justification: Reported average hit@1 changes from 61.5% to 62.0% on synthetic questions and from 56.4% to 55.8% on human-generated questions, under revised configurations and synthetic sampling. V2 adds extensive component and cost results and removes recall@20 from the main baseline comparison. Retained baseline values also change: KAR's MAG hit@5 is 69.6% in v1 Table 4 and 65.4% in v2 Table 3.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.1 corrects the formal definition of NEIGHBORS with the minus sign to use outgoing edges; v1 defines both direction signs using incoming edges. The grounding algorithm is otherwise retained and relocated to Appendix A.3. No new theorems or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: V2 qualifies the broad state-of-the-art claim as superiority over zero- and one-shot methods, acknowledging GraphRAFT's stronger PRIME results with fine-tuning. The headline average first-hit advantage changes from 25.7% to 32.1%, with a different comparison group. The central contributions of modular hybrid retrieval, incremental scope expansion, and alternative rerankers remain.

C2.justification: V2 replaces v1's favorable prose about lenient parsing, which conflicted with v1 Table 7, with support for node-type filtering and a discussion of when edge-type filtering hurts. It adds substantial interpretations of domain and LLM dependence, relational embeddings, schema ambiguity, candidate-cap tradeoffs, and latency. Pairwise reranking is qualified as dataset-dependent rather than uniformly best.

D1.justification: V2 adds the target-type prediction prompt, more explicit relational-context construction and overflow handling, detailed validation defaults, and properties of the evaluated LLMs. Appendix A.6.8 specifies the EPYC 9454 CPU, two A100 80 GB GPUs, vLLM, precomputed embeddings, and timing configurations. These considerably extend v1's basic model, hyperparameter, and prompt disclosures.

R1.justification: V2 adds GraphRAFT and contrasts its fine-tuning and query templates with AF-Retriever's approach. It also adds the Robertson et al. reference for the already-used BM25 baseline and removes the Li, Zhang, and Liu reference. Research positioning more explicitly separates fine-tuned methods from zero- and one-shot approaches, while retaining the overall hybrid SKB retrieval setting.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming the paper and system, v2 extensively rewrites the methodology into problem definitions and an eight-step explanation with a continuous worked example. It reorganizes related work and evaluation, removes duplicated reranking prose, and restructures the appendices into dedicated implementation and analysis subsections.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from two columns to one, redraws the pipeline diagram, and introduces worked-example boxes. It separates aggregate and per-dataset benchmark tables, relocates the grounding algorithm and reference tables to appendices, and adds numerous analysis tables. The original single hit@20 mixture plot becomes paired hit@20/recall@20 validation plots plus corresponding full-test plots.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central candidate-expansion mechanism, component contributions, model dependence, and computational costs through Table 4 and Appendix A.6, addressing important gaps in v1's validation. Full-test evaluation, clearer explanations, additional reproducibility details, and qualification of the state-of-the-art claim further improve the paper. These gains outweigh remaining reporting errors, including Section 4's claim that hiding AMAZON categories hurts performance when Table 16 shows improvement. The changed headline scores themselves do not establish a controlled performance gain.
